armF.summary: Meta rolled back Muse’s human-concierge feature after admitting it had tested contractor calls without proper disclosure.
armF.prompt:
Below is a finished English news feature article (already translated from Japanese, no section headings). Write ONE short, natural sentence that captures the core of the story, in a way a listener can understand by hearing it just once.

Requirements:
- Exactly one sentence.
- Understandable on a single listen.
- Do not pack in multiple separate points; focus on the single most important point or twist of the story.
- Do not add any new fact, conclusion, or lesson that is not already stated in the article below.
- Keep who did what to whom, and what exactly it applied to, the same as in the Japanese source article and the Ledger below.

As a rough guide only (Trial-only guidance, not a strict rule): aim for one main clause with at most one subordinate clause, roughly 12-18 words.

Output only the sentence itself, nothing else (no quotation marks, no label like "In one line:", no Markdown heading markup).

[Article]
# Behind the Scenes of AI Phone Calls: Who Introduces Themselves?

In some calls made through Muse, an experiment was conducted in which trained human contractors, rather than AI, made the calls and completed the conversations with the people they called.

You might say the lead role in the phone call has changed hands. But what matters most is not the voice acting; it is who is on the other end of the line. Wouldn’t that be the first thing you’d want to know?

Meta employees raised privacy concerns that when contractors handle calls, users’ sensitive information could be shared with call center staff without their knowledge. If you thought you were talking to AI but were actually speaking with a person, you might want to know that before deciding what to say.

Then the story took a turn toward, “Maybe this isn’t a good idea.” A Meta vice president admitted it was a mistake to start testing calls by contractors without proper disclosure, and rolled back the human concierge feature for the time being.

A human appears in AI phone calls. It is an intriguing setup, but the main thing to watch this time may not be which one speaks better. Who is on the other end of the phone, and will they clearly say who they are? Before the curtain rises, that may be the first line we want to hear.

[Japanese source article]
AI電話の舞台裏、名乗るのは誰？

Muse経由の電話の一部では、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを完了させる実験が行われました。

電話の主役交代劇、と言いたくなります。けれど、いちばん気になるのは声の演技より、電話口にいるのが誰なのか。あなたなら、まずそこを知りたくなりませんか。

Metaの従業員からは、契約スタッフが電話を担当すると、利用者の機微な情報がコールセンターのスタッフに意図せず共有される可能性がある、というプライバシー上の懸念が示されました。もしAIと話しているつもりで、実は人間が相手だったら。話す内容を決める前に、そのことを知っておきたいと思うかもしれません。

そして、舞台は「それはまずいのでは」という方向へ。Metaの部門副社長は、適切な開示なしに契約スタッフが電話をかけるテストを始めたことをミスと認め、人間コンシェルジュ機能を当面ロールバックしました。

AIの電話に人間が登場する。仕掛けとしては気になりますが、今回の見どころは、どちらが上手に話すかではなさそうです。電話の向こうに誰がいるのか、きちんと名乗ってもらえるか。舞台の幕が上がる前に、まず聞きたいのはそのセリフかもしれません。

armR.final_summary: Meta rolled back its human concierge feature after a vice president called testing without proper disclosure a mistake.
armR.final_text:
# Behind the Scenes of AI Phone Calls: Who Introduces Themselves?

In some calls made through Muse, an experiment was conducted in which trained human contractors, rather than AI, made the calls and completed the conversations with the people they called.

You might say the lead role in the phone call has changed hands. But what matters most is not the voice acting; it is who is on the other end of the line. Wouldn’t that be the first thing you’d want to know?

Meta employees raised privacy concerns that when contractors handle calls, users’ sensitive information could be shared with call center staff without their knowledge. If you thought you were talking to AI but were actually speaking with a person, you might want to know that before deciding what to say.

Then the story took a turn toward, “Maybe this isn’t a good idea.” A Meta vice president admitted it was a mistake to start testing calls by contractors without proper disclosure, and rolled back the human concierge feature for the time being.

A human appears in AI phone calls. It is an intriguing setup, but the main thing to watch this time may not be which one speaks better. Who is on the other end of the phone, and will they clearly say who they are? Before the curtain rises, that may be the first line we want to hear.

## In one line
Meta rolled back its human concierge feature after a vice president called testing without proper disclosure a mistake.
